source_file: Berlin 2026 edition for next app devCon 2026 (flutterCon Berlin), sources listed on the page
question: Q4: The Ugly: AI and the Entry-Level Squeeze

sections.prompt: Raise your hand if your company hired a junior, apprentice or working student developer in the last 12 months.
sections.hint: Indeed DE, Sep 2026: entry-level software postings are 70% below 2019 while apprenticeship postings in the field are 27% above. Ask who trains the next seniors.
no_hands: Where did you get your own first chance, and would that path still exist today?
If you are the student or junior looking for that first chance: what do you hear back, and from whom?
For hirers: why not, no budget, no time to mentor, or do seniors plus AI seem to cover it?
hands_up: How did you find them: apprenticeship (Ausbildung), dual study, university, career change, community?
What does a junior do on your team now that AI writes the first draft?
Did AI make them productive faster, or let them skip understanding?
How do you teach someone to review code they did not write?
follow_ups: If juniors are not hired, where do the seniors come from five years from now?
What should schools and courses stop teaching, and what should they teach more?

sections.prompt: Raise your hand if code written by an agent like Antigravity, Claude Code, Codex or Gemini CLI shipped to your production app this year.
sections.hint: JetBrains, Aug 2026: 90% of professional developers use a coding agent at least weekly. Ask who reviewed the agent's code and how long that took.
no_hands: What stops you: policy, trust, cost, or the code was not good enough?
Do you use AI for anything else in Flutter work: tests, docs, reviews, planning?
For team leads: is there a written rule about agents on your team, and who wrote it?
hands_up: Which Flutter tasks did the agent do well, and where did it fail confidently?
Who reviewed the agent's code, and how long did the review take compared with writing it?
Did agents change how many people the team needs, or just what they do all day?
Does Flutter feel easier or harder for agents than Swift or Kotlin, in your experience?
follow_ups: What is one habit that makes an agent user weaker, and one that makes them stronger?
Which agent setup would you recommend to a Flutter developer starting tomorrow?

sections.prompt: Raise your hand if an agent has written Swift or Kotlin for you this year because you did not want to.
sections.hint: MobileDev-Bench study, Mar 2026: the best AI models fixed 3 to 4% of 407 real mobile issues, mostly Android, no iOS; 5.7% at best when handed the right files. Ask whether native-by-agent felt safe to ship.
no_hands: Who writes the Swift or Kotlin on your project today, and how long do you wait for them?
Which native task would you hand to an agent first?
For the seniors: does cheap native code by agent make Flutter more or less attractive to you?
hands_up: What did it write: a platform channel, a plugin, a whole native module?
Did you understand the code well enough to ship it, and who checked it?
Did it make you more likely to go native next time, or less?
Did anything break in review, on device, or in store review?
follow_ups: If agents make native cheap, what is the remaining argument for one codebase?
Where do you draw the line on shipping code you could not have written?

wrap_up: In a world where agents write the first draft, what should a Flutter developer become excellent at?
What would you tell a student who asks whether to start in mobile at all?
